120	Zalman Shazar remembered the niggun, and he began
121	to return to his roots. There is a long story, we don't have time now, about his self-sacrifice,
122	when they wanted to remove him from his presidency and so on and so on,
123	and maybe on another occasion. But Zalman Shazar told the Rebbe:
124	"Every time I am in a difficult situation, with doubts about what to do,
125	how to do it, I lock myself in a room and play the niggun, and it
126	lights me up, it ignites me."
127	Each one of us has such a niggun.
128	Maybe it is not the same niggun of the Baal HaTanya, but there is some lesson he heard, some
129	talk he heard, some farbrengen of the Rebbe he heard, some word his father said to him,
130	his mother said to him, his teacher said to him.
131	Each of us had some awakening, on Yom Kippur or in some situation,
132	that somewhere deep inside has remained with us. The question is whether
133	we guard it, how we guard it, as a living treasure, so that we
134	remember it, or whether we, God forbid, let it escape from our lives
135	and leave that state. But here comes
136	another very big question. We say that Avraham Avinu came with all the days of his life.
137	But there were times when Avraham Avinu did not keep Torah and mitzvot. He was born
138	in a house that served idols, in Terach's house; he was in the midst of a world
139	of idol worship. And the Rambam describes in the Laws of Idolatry how
140	Avraham Avinu grew up among star-worshippers, and he worshipped idols, and he
141	sold idols at the beginning of his path, until, says the Rambam, he began to investigate,
142	to seek the truth, and after a long, long, long process he arrived
143	at the recognition that there is a Creator of the world. So how can we say
144	that all the days of Avraham Avinu were complete, that he came with all his days?
145	There were years when he did not know the Holy One, blessed be He. Do these years too count
146	as part of his completeness?
147	Avraham Avinu was born into a world that served idols, and that is what he saw
148	in his own home, he saw in the world around him, until he awoke. So how
149	can one say of those days too, when he did not serve
150	the Holy One, blessed be He, until he reached the feeling that there is a Creator of the world,
151	how can it be that these are also holy days?
152	And here comes the great principle.
153	As the Rambam says, he began to wander in his mind, and he was small.
154	Avraham Avinu did not discover the truth in a single moment; he searched, contemplated, investigated,
155	delved deeper, until he came to recognition.
156	And here comes the great novelty.
157	Even these years,
158	when he was an idol worshipper,
159	in the end they too caused him to seek the truth.
160	They were not lost years; they are part of the path by which he arrived.
161	The Torah teaches us that even these years of searching have value,
162	have meaning.
163	Precisely the fact that he did not accept faith as self-evident, but searched on his own,
164	refined himself, gave him the strength to stand against the whole world and say: you
165	are all mistaken, there is a Creator, the Holy One, blessed be He. That is why they call him Avraham HaIvri: the whole world on one side
166	and he on the other side. On the contrary, because he knew what idolatry is,
167	he knew the way of thinking of these people, and so he knew how
168	to speak with them, how to influence them, how to lead them to faith
169	in the Holy One, blessed be He. And this is the meaning of "Avraham was old, advanced in days."
170	Avraham did not arrive only with the days in which he was already the great one of the generation.
171	He came also with the years of searching, of doubts; all these years are part of the building
172	of his personality, of his mission.
173	One day Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev met
174	a great, famous wicked man.
175	Instead of keeping away from him or rebuking him for what he does, he says to him
176	a very surprising sentence: "I envy you."
177	Then the man says: "Rebbe, what do you envy
178	in me?"
179	He says to him: "You have committed many transgressions, but we know that if someone
180	repents out of love, the intentional sins become merits. I
181	envy you.
182	You will have so many merits that I cannot dream of having them."
183	Each one of us, our life is like a book.
184	Each stage is like another chapter.
185	Each of us has certain chapters in the book of his life that he would like to erase,
186	rewrite from the beginning,
187	write differently.
188	But we all know the past:
189	the past, we have no control over it.
190	And sometimes we think to ourselves: if we could start life over, oh oh oh, we would
191	do this or that or that.
192	But we actually have two options for how to relate to our falls,
193	to the past in which we failed.
194	We can keep thinking: I have no strength.
195	I am a person who fails, I am incapable, I always spoil things.
196	And then our past becomes the one that rules over us.
197	It rules over us, it brings us down.
198	Even if this event happened many years ago, it rules over our lives.
199	But there are people who think completely differently.
200	I failed?
201	What can I learn from this?
202	What do I know today that I did not know then?
203	How can I use this experience, my fall, to become a more elevated person, a
204	better person?
205	For him the past does not rule, it does not bring him down; it is his teacher, his guide,
206	his rabbi.
207	And so there are people who, the more they age, become more open, deeper,
208	more patient, more powerful.
209	The experience made them people who understand more about themselves,
210	about others, about life.
211	What is the difference?
212	They did with the past years what you do.
213	This experience made you wiser.
214	There are people whom experience made bitter of spirit, an irritable person.
215	But there are people who tell themselves: do not throw away yesterday, but do not dwell
216	in it, you do not live in it; you take from it the light, you take from it the wisdom.
217	Take from it what you learned and keep walking forward.
218	A person who went through bad times and overcame them can influence his friend more.
219	…
220	If he sees a person who is in the same situation he was in, he says: "I understand you very well.
221	I too was in that place.
222	I too had the same questions, the same falls, the same challenges.
223	But I want to tell you what I discovered about myself."
224	And if HaShem helps us, and each of us has had times when he overcame a certain situation,
225	a challenging test, we need to use it
226	to help awaken other people.
227	Each one of us, now that we are
228	sitting together and hearing
229	this wonderful thing,
230	each one of us should think now: what things in my life were challenges for me
231	and I overcame them?
232	What things gave me strength to cope?
233	What wisdom did you learn?
234	What wisdom did I receive from these challenges?
235	And to give, to tell, to pass on to other people,
236	to give to other people today who are more or less in the same situation, to let them
237	help them.
238	Personally, in my life I had many things that were great challenges for me,
239	and I learned from them.
